summary: When several PIM routers share a LAN, they can forward duplicate multicast packets, so PIM Assert messages elect one forwarder per flow. This document defines a PackedAssert message that carries Assert information for multiple flows at once. This reduces the number of PIM packets on the LAN and can speed up the election.

plainLanguage.summary: Many kids might all try to hand out the same flyers. They hold a quick vote to pick one. This lets them vote on lots of flyers in one go instead of one by one.

questions: how do pim routers elect a multicast forwarder
subtitle: One PIM message that carries the Assert information for many multicast flows at once.

tldr.problem: When several PIM routers share a LAN, they can forward duplicate multicast packets, and each flow needs its own small Assert message to elect one forwarder. With many flows, routers can be swamped and duplicates last longer.
tldr.mechanism: PackedAssert messages put the assert records of many flows into one PIM message, either as plain repeated records or in two aggregated forms. A new Hello option announces support, and the Assert state machine is not changed.
tldr.outcome: Fewer, larger packets can speed up the election of a single forwarder and reduce duplicate multicast traffic. It is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted.

today: RFC 9466 is a Proposed Standard published in October 2023. The metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
On a shared LAN with more than one upstream router, the same multicast packet can show up from several routers. PIM-SM (RFC 7761) fixes this with Assert messages that elect a single forwarder. Each Assert carries one multicast source and group, plus the Metric and Metric Preference of the route towards the source or the Rendezvous Point (RP). Asserts are also sent periodically to keep the Assert state alive.

This RFC defines the PackedAssert message, which encodes the information of several Asserts in one packet. It changes no Assert state machinery. It only cuts the number of PIM packets on the LAN, which can speed up the election and reduce duplicate packets, especially with many groups or when the routers process PIM packets slowly.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of shouting one note per flyer, the kids bundle many notes into one envelope. Fewer envelopes means everyone finishes sorting things out faster.

sections.title: The Problem with Many Asserts
sections.content:
As long as a Layer 2 network connects more than two PIM routers, there may be several upstream routers, duplicate traffic and Assert processing. As multicast services grow, a data burst can trigger a large number of small Assert packets in a short time. The routers must process all of them, may not keep up, and may even discard some. That extends the time during which traffic is duplicated.

The only way to avoid Asserts is to build the network without transit subnets that have several upstream routers, for example by turning an L2 ring into a ring of point-to-point subnets. The RFC explains why that is often undesirable: it raises the cost of introducing IP multicast, and some L2 technologies are needed, such as rings with sub-50 msec failover or IEEE Time-Sensitive Networking.

Appendix A lists settings where many asserts are seen or expected: enterprise networks, video surveillance, financial services, IPTV broadcast video, multicast VPN distribution trees and future TSN or DetNet underlays.
sections.plainLanguage: If too many kids shout at once, the teacher cannot hear them all and the mess lasts longer. Making everyone stand in single file would fix it, but sometimes the playground just is not built that way.

sections.title: Announcing Support with a Hello Option
sections.content:
Routers announce support with the PIM Packed Assert Capability Hello option, which is OptionType 40 with OptionLength 0 and no value. It says the router can receive and process every PackedAssert encoding in this document.

PackedAssert messages MUST NOT be used unless all PIM routers on the subnet announce the option. If any router on the LAN has not signaled support, implementations MUST only send ordinary Asserts.
sections.plainLanguage: Before using the bundled envelopes, everyone in the room has to say they know how to read them. If even one kid does not, they all go back to single notes.

sections.title: PackedAssert Message Formats
sections.content:
An assert record is the information in one Assert: the R flag, Source Address, Group Address, Metric and Metric Preference. Two flags in the PIM Assert message header (defined with RFC 9436) pick the encoding. P is the Packed flag and A is the Aggregated flag. With P=0 the message is a normal Assert and A MUST be 0. With P=1 it is a PackedAssert.

  • P=1, A=0: a Simple PackedAssert, a sequence of ordinary assert records, after a header with a Zero field and a Reserved field.
  • P=1, A=1: an Aggregated PackedAssert, a sequence of aggregated assert records.

A Source Aggregated Assert Record has R=0 and carries one Source Address, Metric and Metric Preference with a list of Group Addresses, so it stands for (S,G1) to (S,Gn). The Source Address MUST NOT be zero.

An RP Aggregated Assert Record has R=1 and carries one Metric and Metric Preference with a list of Group Records. Each Group Record has a Group Address and zero or more Source Addresses. It covers (*,G) records that share the same metric, which normally means the same RP. The RP address itself is not encoded.

The Zero field is set to zero on transmission so that a router that does not support packing fails to parse the message instead of mis-parsing it as a normal Assert. The number of records is not carried; it is derived from the packet length.
sections.plainLanguage: A bundled envelope can hold plain notes one after another, or notes grouped by who they are about. Grouping saves space because you write the name only once.

sections.title: Sending and Receiving PackedAsserts
sections.content:
PackedAsserts do not change the PIM Assert state machine. When the state machine would send an Assert, an implementation MAY instead remember the assert record and later build PackedAsserts from the remembered records. Regular Assert messages are still allowed. When PackedAsserts are used is out of scope for the RFC.

Reception-triggered records, caused by data arrival or by Asserts received while in the "I am Assert Winner" state, are time critical. The router SHOULD send them as soon as possible, with higher priority than other records and bypassing bursty PIM messages such as join/prune. If nothing is already being sent, it should send immediately without further packing.

Timer-triggered records are not urgent. The Assert_Override_Interval already gives a 3-second window. As an example, an implementation can round the Assert Timer to a granularity such as 100 msec so that many states expire together and pack easily. AssertCancel messages can be packed too.

A lost PackedAssert affects every flow in it, so routers SHOULD support sending Asserts with a DSCP such as Expedited Forwarding. They MAY offer an option to send a PackedAssert twice in short order, such as 50 msec apart, if the two together are smaller than the equivalent Asserts and no replies are expected. The best packing size depends on the implementation, and past a point larger packets bring more duplicates on loss.

On receipt, the router converts the payload into assert records and processes them as if equivalent Asserts had arrived. Implementations SHOULD also let operators see counts of Assert and PackedAssert messages and records, and SHOULD provide a way to disable PackedAssert.
sections.plainLanguage: If a problem is urgent, send the note right away on its own. If it is just a routine reminder, wait a moment and bundle it with others. The person reading unpacks the envelope and treats each note as if it came alone.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security considerations of RFC 7761 apply. A forged Assert can make the legitimate forwarder stop forwarding to the LAN, and the effect may be amplified with a PackedAssert because it covers many flows.

Because the extension is active only when all routers signal support, one misconfigured or malicious router sending forged Hello messages can inhibit it. Authenticating PIM messages, as explained in Sections 6.2 and 6.3 of RFC 7761, can protect against forged messages.
sections.plainLanguage: A fake note in a bundle can cause more trouble than one fake note alone. Checking who really wrote the notes keeps the game fair.

sections.title: IANA Considerations
sections.content: IANA added Hello option 40, "Packed Assert Capability", with length 0, to the PIM-Hello Options registry. In the "PIM Message Types" registry, for type 5 (Assert), IANA assigned flag bit 0 as Packed and flag bit 1 as Aggregated. Bits 2 to 7 remain unassigned.
sections.plainLanguage: The official list of PIM signals got two new switches and one new announcement card.

fields.name: R
fields.desc: MUST be 0: all represented records are (S,G).

fields.name: Source Address
fields.desc: Encoded-Unicast format; MUST NOT be zero.

fields.name: Number of Groups (N)
fields.desc: How many Group Address fields follow.

fields.name: Reserved
fields.desc: Zero on transmission, ignored on receipt.
